network_thesis.headline: One app. Korea's coasts, rivers and islands. The water layer of Kakao T.
network_thesis.body: Korea is a peninsula wrapped in water — a megacity river (the Han), beach-and-bay metros (Busan), marquee islands (Jeju), a national marine park (Hallyeohaesang), and international corridors to Japan — and Kakao Mobility (Kakao T) is the dominant mobility app that owns the demand and the in-app wallet across all of it. The same in-app foiling tier proven in the Maldives extends to Korea's busiest water surfaces: pick one market to prove it, or roll the recommended sequence below.
network_thesis.how_to_read: Each card is a real, ready market. Start with Busan — the most renderable, ready pilot — or pick any cluster. Seoul / the Han River is the strategic hero. The phased sequence is our recommended path, not the only one.

partner_context.their_ambition: You are Kakao Mobility (Kakao T) — the dominant Korean mobility platform, the ride-hail and multimodal core of the Kakao ecosystem (KakaoTalk ≈ 97% messaging share). You unveiled a global ride-hailing app in 2024 courting inbound demand across ~30 countries, and you are actively widening your multimodal map.
partner_context.their_pressure: Land ride-hail in Korea is maturing and contested. Your next leg of high-margin growth comes from new surfaces — and Korea's water is a megacity river, beach-and-bay metros, marquee islands and international corridors, none of which any mobility app has ever monetized. Seoul's 2025 Hangang Bus launch under-delivered on speed, leaving the river open.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Water is the mobility surface Kakao doesn't own yet. Navier turns it into a tier in Kakao T: a software-defined foiling fleet, booked in-app, premium-priced, on the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju's islets, the Hallyeohaesang marine park and the cross-border corridors to Japan — the same network model already ramping in the Maldives.

hero.title: Kakao Mobility × Navier — Korea's water, in the app
hero.subtitle: Korea is a peninsula wrapped in water and Kakao T is its mobility app. The water is the surface no one owns yet.
hero.what_we_do_together: We launch a Kakao-T-booked foiling water tier across Korea's busiest water surfaces — the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju's islets, the Hallyeohaesang marine park, and the cross-border corridors to Japan. Navier brings the software-defined hydrofoiling fleet and the network playbook now proven in the Maldives; Kakao Mobility brings the demand, the app, the wallet, and home-turf reach across Korea. Together we turn slow river buses and aging ferries into fast, smooth, all-weather in-app water trips.

why_now: Foiling lifts the hull clear of the water: faster, dramatically more efficient per passenger-mile, smooth and near-silent, hybrid-capable with no charging dependency, and autonomy-ready. A ~100-vessel network is already ramping in the Maldives, and Korea's water is wide open — Seoul's 2025 Hangang Bus launch was criticised as too slow, Busan's waterfront has no in-app tier, and Jeju's islet ferries are aging. The category gets claimed cluster-by-cluster.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop - roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists - the Han River piers, Busan's harbour, Jeju's ports and the marine-park terminals. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all for the cross-border legs.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces converge in Kakao's backyard: the technology crossed from prototype to platform; a ~100-vessel network is ramping in the Maldives; and Korea's water surfaces — a slow new river bus, an un-monetized Busan bay, aging Jeju ferries — are ready to be switched onto a clean foiling tier in the app Koreans already live in.
wow_corridors: Han River foiling commute (the fast answer to the slow Hangang Bus)
Busan bay hops + the Busan↔Fukuoka cross-border line-haul
Jeju islet runs (Udo / Marado / Gapado) + the mainland line-haul

multimodal_fit: Kakao Mobility already runs the hardest parts: real-time demand, dispatch, dynamic pricing, navigation, payments and a taxi-hailing network across Korea. A foiling water tier slots straight in — same app, same wallet, captain-partners instead of driver-partners, the water leg booked door-to-door with the Kakao T ride to and from the pier.

differentiation.why_navier: Software-defined and autonomy-ready — the same software-first instincts Kakao brings. A ~100-vessel at-scale network already proving the model in the Maldives, directly relevant to Korea's many-island, river-and-coast geography.

proof_points.claim: Kakao Mobility (Kakao T) is Korea's dominant mobility platform.
proof_points.evidence: Kakao T was the clear ride-hail market leader with ~13.2 million monthly active users (rivals far behind), spanning taxi-hailing, navigation, proxy-driver, parking and bike — the demand and the in-app wallet a water tier slots straight into.

proof_points.claim: Kakao is a super-app at national scale, actively widening its multimodal and global map.
proof_points.evidence: KakaoTalk reaches ~93% of Korea's population; Kakao's platform segment (which houses Kakao Mobility) booked ₩993.0B revenue in Q1 2025 (+4% YoY), and Kakao Mobility launched a global inbound ride-hailing app across ~30 countries in 2024.
proof_points.source: Kakao Corp Q1 2025 earnings (May 2025) + Kakao IR

proof_points.claim: Korea's regulators are pulling marine fleets toward clean propulsion.
proof_points.evidence: Korea's national 'Toward Green Shipping by 2050' plan / 2030 Greenship-K strategy mandates eco-friendly conversion of public vessels and targets ~118 eco-friendly ships converted by 2030 on the path to net-zero domestic shipping by 2050 — a direct tailwind for a clean foiling tier.
proof_points.source: Korea Ministry of Oceans & Fisheries / Argus Media, 2023

proof_points.claim: Seoul's own river-transport push proves Han River demand — and the speed gap Navier fills.
proof_points.evidence: Seoul's ₩150B (~$105M) Hangang Bus launched in September 2025 and passed 300,000 cumulative riders within months, but drew divided reviews and was widely criticised as too slow to be real transport — exactly the fast-foiling-tier opening.
proof_points.source: Korea Times / Korea Herald / Straits Times, 2025–2026

objections.concern: Is the range enough across Korea's water?
objections.response: Korea's water splits cleanly into short hops and long line-hauls. The Han River commute (~11 nm), Busan's bay (~4 nm), Jeju's islets (~4–6 nm) and the Hallyeohaesang marine park (~12–30 nm) all sit well inside the Pioneer II / N35 70 nm all-electric envelope; the Busan↔Fukuoka (~110 nm) and Jeju↔Busan (~157 nm) line-hauls run on the Quanta-LR hybrid (700 nm, no charging infrastructure required).

objections.concern: Why succeed on the Han River where the Hangang Bus underwhelmed?
objections.response: The river bus is a slow conventional craft criticised as not-real-transport; a 30+ kt foiling tier is a different product entirely — a genuine cross-city commute, premium-priced and on demand in the Kakao T app Seoulites already use.

objections.concern: Korea's winters, monsoon and typhoon season cut operating days.
objections.response: Foils ride above the chop and software-defined routing flexes with conditions, so the fleet runs smooth on days conventional ferries cancel; demand concentrates in the long beach-and-islet seasons the fleet is sized for, while the cross-border and business line-hauls carry year-round flow.

objections.concern: Is the network model proven enough to commit to?
objections.response: A ~100-vessel, $100M, 3-year network is already ramping with JIH Global in the Maldives, and a second island-network anchor is signed with the WorldBridge Group in Cambodia — the same software-defined, autonomy-ready foiling model, directly relevant to Korea's river, coast and many-island geography.

phases.label: Phase 1 — Busan beachhead
phases.rationale: Start where the water demand is densest, most renderable and ready — Busan's beach-and-bay waterfront, with captive ferry demand and ready piers.
phases.narrative: Busan is the proof market: a scenic beach-and-bay shoreline with no in-app water tier. A small Pioneer II / N35 fleet on the Haeundae–Gwangalli–Marine City hops and the Geoje run shows Kakao T users a water layer that feels like the rest of the app.

phases.label: Phase 2 — Jeju + the cross-border line-haul
phases.rationale: Layer in Korea's marquee island-tourism market (Jeju islet hops + resort arrivals) and the marquee international corridor (Busan↔Fukuoka) the Quanta-LR hybrid was built for.
phases.narrative: Jeju turns the story to premium leisure — all-weather islet hops and resort arrivals — while the Busan↔Fukuoka Quanta-LR line-haul opens the cross-border flow inside an app travellers on both sides hold.

phases.label: Phase 3 — the south-coast marine park + the Han River
phases.rationale: Carry the network into the Hallyeohaesang marine-park island-hopping mesh and the Jeju↔mainland line-haul, and stand up the strategic Han River commute once the Seoul map node is built.
phases.narrative: The south coast is where the island mesh matters — Yeosu, Tongyeong and their marine-park islands — and the Han River is the strategic hero: a fast foiling commute that turns Seoul's slow river bus into real transport.

phases.label: Phase 4 — the whole Korean water map
phases.rationale: With the clusters proven, knit them into one national in-app water tier across Korea's coasts, river and cross-border corridors.
phases.narrative: The end state: Kakao T's foiling water tier across the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju, the Hallyeohaesang marine park and the cross-border corridors to Japan — one app, Korea's water.

This is the most renderable, ready Kakao T water market: urban bay hops, a Geoje commuter run, and an all-weather cross-border line-haul to Japan.

end_state.headline: The water layer of Korea's mobility app — coast, river and islands, nationwide.
end_state.addressable_footprint: Every Korean water surface Kakao T already serves on land — the Han River through 10M-person Seoul, Busan's beach-and-bay metro, Jeju's island-tourism coast, the Hallyeohaesang marine park, and the cross-border corridors to Japan.

steady_state.platform_mix: Pioneer II / N35 for the river, bay and islet capillaries + Quanta-LR for the Jeju and cross-border line-hauls
steady_state.tam_framing: Jeju alone drew ~13.9M visitors in 2025, Seoul is a 10M-person megacity, and the Korea–Japan strait carries year-round business and tourism flow — all running today on slow river buses and aging ferries, a premium water-mobility surface no app has monetised.

end_state.narrative: Steady state is not a pilot count — it is the whole Korean water map. Busan proves the model, then Jeju and the cross-border line-haul, the Hallyeohaesang marine park, and the strategic Han River: 410 foiling vessels across four clusters, on 20+ corridors, booked entirely inside Kakao T — Pioneer II / N35 for the river, bay and islet capillaries and Quanta-LR for the long Jeju and Japan legs. The Maldives' ~100-vessel network is the unit; Korea is that model brought home to a peninsula wrapped in water — the water layer of the app Koreans already live in.
